header.tag_why: Raj told Tom the competitor pitched one platform for the tills and the website on one contract, and 11 of the customer's 14 post-meeting questions were about stores. Our unified-commerce slide was called 'a diagram', and we only described the till return, never showed it. Champion or access is the runner-up because Angela signed with Adyen and Tom met her once.

messaging_changes.current_line: Online and in-store on one platform; the line between them has pretty much disappeared.
messaging_changes.change: Replace the abstract claim with the customer's own terms and a concrete scenario. For example: 'One system for the tills and the website: one customer, one basket. Watch an online order returned at a store till.' Back it with a live or recorded return walk-through.
messaging_changes.why: The head of store operations dismissed the slide as 'a diagram' and asked how a return works at the till. The customer's own phrases were concrete, and none of them was 'unified commerce'.
evidence_excerpts: One system for the tills and the website.
We described it. We never showed it.

messaging_changes.change: Add a store-rollout line that answers the questions retailers ask: dates, who installs, what happens to the old tills, what happens when store wifi drops, and who shows up when a till goes down on a Saturday. Only claim what we can actually staff and show.
messaging_changes.why: The store ops workshop is where the deal turned. We had no rollout plan and no one who had run a store rollout. Our answer on installs was 'a partner', against a competitor who reportedly brought a retail team.
evidence_excerpts: Then a rollout plan. Dates, who installs, what happens to the old tills.
Nobody on our side had run a store rollout.
I said we'd bring in a partner.

messaging_changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
messaging_changes.change: Replace generic customer stories with a retailer reference the prospect can actually call, ideally one running stores and online, plus a short return walk-through from that retailer.
messaging_changes.why: The COO's response to our case study was to ask for a call, and we couldn't arrange one in time. A written story did not satisfy her. The competitor reportedly named retailers she knew.

evidence.excerpt: The store couldn't see the online order, so staff were refunding to gift cards or telling people to mail it back.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: they'd just launched a loyalty program that was supposed to work everywhere and didn't, because store and web were two different customer records.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Their COO, Angela, apparently stood in a store on December 27th watching the returns queue.
evidence.label: opinion

trigger.insight: The trigger was an operational failure in stores: returns and a loyalty program that broke because web and store customer records were separate. It was not a checkout or conversion problem. The December 27th scene is hearsay ('apparently', 'the story everybody there tells'). It still shows the COO, a store-side owner, felt the pain personally, which fits her later signing. We opened and won on web, but the problem was in the stores.
trigger.messaging: Lead with the post-purchase, in-store pain (returns, one customer record across loyalty and refunds) instead of global growth or developer speed.

evidence.excerpt: The CTO, Raj. He ran the RFP, he was my contact the whole way.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Once. The kickoff.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: ...Probably Angela. Raj wanted us. I think. He told me he did.
evidence.label: opinion

decider.insight: Tom's first answer was Raj, but when asked who signed with Adyen he said Angela, and then retreated to 'Probably Angela'. We built the deal around the RFP runner and had one meeting with the person who held the signature. Raj's support is known only because Raj said so. So the decider is likely the COO, whose team asked for the store workshop, but this is Tom's inference rather than something he observed.
decider.messaging: Messaging must reach the business owner of the store problem, not only the technical evaluator. Build COO-level proof around returns, rollout and reference calls.

evidence.excerpt: He said they came in with a retail team, people who'd done store rollouts, and they talked about one platform for the tills and the website, on one contract.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Before, it was all web. Conversion, checkout, wallets. After, it was stores.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Raj forwarded me a list of 14 questions and 11 of them were about stores.
evidence.label: fact

competitor.insight: Tom wasn't in the competitor's meeting, so this is Raj's account. The documented change is the 14-question list, where 11 are about stores. The customer moved from checkout questions to wifi outages, a 120-store rollout and till support. The competitor's reported strengths are the people (a retail team with rollout experience), the promise (one platform, one contract) and the references (retailers Angela knew). Not one of these is a product-feature claim.
competitor.messaging: Compete on retail credibility, meaning people who have done store rollouts, retail references and a single contract. A feature comparison will not answer this.

evidence.excerpt: Reaction: the online checkout demo. Their ecommerce lead loved it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: that's a diagram.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Then she asked how a return works. Step by step. At the till.
evidence.label: fact

message.insight: Our online checkout demo landed with the ecommerce lead, which is the audience that was already ours. The unified commerce line met silence from the store operations head, who called it 'a diagram' and asked for a step-by-step return at the till. Tom's answer to that, 'I described it', repeated the slide in words. Our claim was one the customer wanted to see done, and we couldn't show it.
message.messaging: Replace the unified-commerce claim with a demonstrated return flow in the customer's terms. Keep the checkout demo for the ecommerce audience, but don't count its reaction as progress on the store question.

evidence.excerpt: Nobody on our side had run a store rollout.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: She wrote something down and didn't ask another question.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I knew on the drive home.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Right before that, honestly, we were ahead. Raj said so. We'd won the web side.
evidence.label: opinion

decided.insight: The turning point was the store ops workshop. Six store operations people faced our solutions engineer and Tom, and no one on our side had run a store rollout. When asked who does the installs, Tom said a partner. Bev's silence is Tom's read, not a stated verdict, but the later asks (reference call, rollout plan, live return) fit it. 'We were ahead' rests on Raj, who was the web-side contact. Winning the web side did not matter once the buyer shifted to stores.
decided.messaging: Treat store credibility as the deciding point. Be ready for a store-operations workshop with someone who has run rollouts, a rollout plan and a live return demo.

evidence.excerpt: can I talk to them?
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Then a rollout plan. Dates, who installs, what happens to the old tills.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: They wanted to watch an online order get returned at a store till, live.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: We described it. We never showed it.
evidence.label: fact

gaps.insight: There were three gaps, and all were about proof rather than product features. We had no retailer the COO could speak to in time, no rollout plan (dates, installer, old tills), and no live return demo. Tom doesn't say we couldn't do returns, only that we never showed it. Whether the capability exists is not established, and that matters for what we can claim.
gaps.messaging: Prepare a callable retail reference, a standard rollout plan template and a repeatable live return demo before making claims about stores.

evidence.excerpt: One system for the tills and the website.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: I don't want two vendors pointing at each other.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: one customer, one basket.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: They never said "unified commerce." We kept saying "in-person payments" and "point of sale." They said "the tills."
evidence.label: fact

language.insight: The customer's words were plain and operational: 'the tills', one system, one customer, one basket, and no two vendors pointing at each other. Our own words ('unified commerce', 'in-person payments', 'point of sale') were not theirs. Angela's quote shows the fear is accountability across vendors, not features. Bev repeated the one-system phrase every time, so it was a consistent ask.
language.messaging: Use 'the tills', 'one system', 'one customer, one basket' and single-vendor accountability in copy and talk tracks, and drop 'unified commerce' as the lead term for retail.

gaps.question: Who made the final call, and how do you know?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom what he actually saw (signature, email, call) from Angela, and whether Raj ever told him directly why they chose Adyen. Ask Raj, or anyone else on the buying side, for a debrief.

gaps.question: What did the customer's incumbent set-up look like?
gaps.follow_up: Ask who the incumbent was for tills and for web, and what contract or timing constraints the 'old tills' created.

gaps.question: What did the competitor actually show or promise (live return demo, rollout plan, references)?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Raj, or Tom's contacts, what Adyen presented at the store meetings and whether they demoed a return. Tom only has Raj's account.

gaps.question: Can we actually do the till return, and could we have shown it?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom and the solutions engineer why the live return was never shown: was it a product limit, an environment issue or a lack of preparation?

close.rep_takeaway: When the buyer's questions change, follow them. After the questions turned to stores, we kept selling the web strength and met the person who signed only once. Get to the signer early, and bring the store experience, reference and live demo that her team asks for.
